articleSummary: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD) peaks in autumn and winter in China, caused by enteroviruses, mainly Enterovirus 71 (EV71) and Coxsackievirus A16. Incubation is 2–14 days (typically 3–5). Infected children, usually under 5, present with vesicular rashes on hands, feet, and buttocks, oral ulcers with drooling, and fever with possible cough and runny nose; appetite loss may occur. Most cases are mild and self-limiting within about a week, but EV71 can cause severe neurologic, respiratory, or circulatory complications. Seek urgent care for high fever, altered mental status, seizures, or abnormal heart rate or breathing. Transmission is fecal-oral, via contact with contaminated hands, objects, surfaces, and via respiratory droplets. Prevention emphasizes thorough handwashing (seven-step method), ventilation, and surface disinfection; avoid crowded indoor places during peak seasons; children with HFMD should stay home. An inactivated EV71 vaccine is available for ages 6 months–5 years, but it does not protect against other enteroviruses; continue preventive measures post-vaccination.

articleHeadline: Genomics Moves to the Front Line of Malaria Surveillance
articleSummary: As of 2026-10-15, malaria molecular surveillance has moved from concept to a programmatic backbone of WHO's malaria elimination strategy. Genotyping enables distinguishing imported versus locally acquired infections, tracking transmission clusters, and monitoring drug resistance. Programs now use high-throughput sequencing, targeted panels, and portable platforms to meet operational needs. Key approaches include a highly multiplexed molecular inversion probe panel for Plasmodium falciparum, and SNP barcode panels for P. falciparum and P. vivax, validated against traditional markers in the Peruvian Amazon. Portable Oxford Nanopore sequencing has been deployed in Nigeria to profile resistance loci in antenatal care settings, and targeted mosquito genotyping improves species assignment across Anopheles. Translation to practice shows heterogeneity in Tanzania mainland and warns that P. vivax transmission can rebound (Papua New Guinea). In Vietnam (2018–2020), artemisinin-based therapy resistance spread during a malaria decline, underscoring the need for genomic-informed containment and treatment guidance. Barriers remain cost, infrastructure, and skilled personnel.

articleSummary: Six bacteriophages (φRAGS1, φRAGS8, φRAGS15, φRAGS21, φRAGS37, φRAGS47) showed broad lytic activity against MRSA clinical isolates, with φRAGS15 lysing all 17 strains. articleSummary: SAGE October 2026 recommendations on inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) use in routine immunization and outbreak response: countries with fewer than three IPV doses should switch promptly to a three-dose IPV-containing schedule, delivering the third dose preferably via hexavalent vaccines. If a poliovirus outbreak persists beyond six months after an initial fractional or full IPV dose, a second IPV dose in outbreak response may be considered to boost mucosal immunity, with a short-to-medium-term program evaluation. IPV remains the only vaccine protecting against all three poliovirus serotypes and type 2, which is currently most prevalent in circulation; modelling shows median type 2 immunity among under-fives at ~60% in 2025, ~70% by 2031 under the two-dose schedule, below the ~80% transmission-protection threshold. A third IPV dose could raise end-of-series immunity to ~99% with a 6-10-14 week schedule (vs ~78% with fewer doses), with largest gains in high-risk settings like Nigeria, DRC, Pakistan, and Chad. Hexavalent co-formulation is preferred for reducing visits and costs; ~40 Gavi-eligible countries are expected to switch, Mauritania and Senegal have started. Supply is projected sufficient: IPV and hexavalent capacity exceed demand; ~55 million additional doses/year across 40+ high-risk countries, timing is critical to ensure lead times and reach unvaccinated children.

articleSummary: Single-center retrospective study at Shanxi Children’s Hospital, Taiyuan, China, reviewing 123 pediatric septic shock patients admitted to PICU from 2020–2024, with 28‑day mortality of 83/123 (67.5%). articleSummary: Ebola response funds in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) remain opaque: more than $700 million could not be traced. Donors say about $962 million reached response partners, but evaluators could account for only $228 million; of that, roughly $127 million had been spent, with the rest in recipients’ control. Kinshasa-based Africa CDC Director Jean Kaseya said fewer than 30% of organizations submitted reports; officials will investigate how funds were allocated and what work was performed. Absence of spend data does not prove theft, but signals opaque management. Organizations that refuse disclosure risk loss of accreditation and possible inclusion on a continental blacklist. The May 2026 Ebola outbreak in the DRC has exceeded 9,000 confirmed cases and 4,300 deaths, the largest on record; MSF notes accelerating spread in North Kivu, with about 40% of new cases in September there and 34% treated in general facilities, not specialized centers.

articleSummary: Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of Congo faces financial transparency challenges, according to Africa CDC Director-General Dr. Jean Kaseya. articleHeadline: Licensed Ebola Vaccine Ervebo Triggered T Cells Against Bundibugyo in 13 of 20 Recipients, but Protection Remains Unproven
articleSummary: Ervebo, the licensed Ebola vaccine, elicited Bundibugyo-cross reactive T cells in 13 of 20 adults 28 days after a single dose. Sixteen recipients had T cells reacting to Zaire ebolavirus and seven to Sudan virus proteins; Bundibugyo and Zaire surface proteins share roughly 66% identity, helping explain cross-reactivity. The small healthy-volunteer study, published in The Lancet Infectious Diseases, does not measure protection and did not follow exposed individuals. Bundibugyo drives the Democratic Republic of the Congo outbreak, with Bunia in Ituri province a focal point; as of Oct 14, 2026, there were 9,167 confirmed cases and 4,413 deaths globally, with Congo at 9,144/4,410, Uganda 20/2 plus one probable, Kenya 2/1, and France 1 case (no deaths). WHO guidance remains unchanged, recommending vaccine use within research protocols. About 70,000 doses were allocated to Congo; 20,000 for a phase 3 trial in Bunia (Sept 19), vaccinating exposed health workers. US risk remains very low; CDC directs enhanced screening for travelers and returning workers.

articleHeadline: Onion Extract Boosts Standard Therapy Against Latent Tuberculosis in Rabbit
articleSummary: Latent-like pulmonary infection by Mycobacterium aurum in New Zealand White rabbits was used to test Allium cepa (onion) extract as an adjunct to standard TB preventive therapy. In Kumasi, Ghana, researchers induced latency, validated by stabilized lung CFU, chest radiographs without active disease, and adaptive immune changes. During four weeks of treatment, rabbits received isoniazid plus rifapentine, onion extract (250/500/1000 mg/kg), or both. All onion-containing regimens reduced pulmonary bacterial burden vs untreated controls (P<0.0001). The combination with the highest onion dose yielded the greatest reduction: 480 CFU vs 495 CFU for uninfected controls, suggesting near-complete clearance. The study supports plant-derived compounds as adjuncts to latent TB therapy, potentially via improved drug uptake, efflux-pump inhibition, or complementary metabolic targeting; prior in vitro work showed anti-efflux and antibiofilm effects of Allium cepa extracts.

articleSummary: Malaria in Ghana’s Agogo cohort: platelet counts decline with age, complicating thrombocytopenia interpretation and allowing no clear sex difference, suggesting age-aware rather than sex-based thresholds. Seasonal positivity peaks in May–June during Ghana’s rainy season in forest–savanna transition zones, in a high-transmission setting (inoculation rate 40–158 bites/person/year). Non-parametric methods and Spearman correlations analyzed median (IQR) platelet counts and parasite densities.

articleSummary: Pneumonic plague outbreak in Northeast China began autumn–winter 1910, spreading from the Russia–Siberia border into Manchuria along the Chinese Eastern Railway, with Harbin's Fujiadian district hardest hit. Cambridge-trained Wu Liande (31) returned to lead the response, performing autopsies to prove airborne transmission, introducing the Wu mask (gauze mask), establishing zoned control, isolation hospitals, and cremating mass graves to halt spread. By March 1911, deaths in the Harbin area were zero; an International Plague Conference in Fengtian (Shenyang) chaired by Wu Liande acknowledged China’s anti-epidemic efforts, catalyzing modern public health. Today, rumors of a Russian plague-lab leak are unfounded; authorities report no outbreak. Plague remains Class A in China; maintain vigilance, avoid contact with wild marmots, and rely on official sources to counter misinformation.

articleHeadline: Months of Hallucinations Led Doctors to Tapeworm Cysts in a Woman's Brain, and Pork Wasn't How She Got Them
articleSummary: Neurocysticercosis from pork tapeworm eggs infected a 52-year-old woman in the Philippines, presenting four months of headaches and visual hallucinations, then speech and naming difficulties. Brain MRI/CT showed cysts in multiple lobes and the cerebellum, each with a bright dot—the scolex—producing the pathognomonic dot-in-hole sign. EEG revealed epileptiform discharges on the left posterior cortex, linking hallucinations to seizures. Infection arises from swallowing tapeworm eggs shed in human feces, not from eating pork; eggs hatch and form brain cysts, with symptoms often appearing months to years later as cysts die. She was treated with praziquantel and albendazole, glucocorticoids, and levetiracetam; steroids curb inflammation from dying cysts. After one month, symptoms resolved and cysts shrank with dots disappearing. Neurocysticercosis is common where pigs roam and sanitation is poor (Latin America, Asia, Africa) and is a leading cause of adult-onset epilepsy globally. CDC emphasizes handwashing, safe food/water, and travel history in diagnosis.
